catalog_quote: p. 9, §2.3 Tone: "There are four tone levels in Jɔ. Although most Mande languages have two tone levels, four-level systems are not unknown, e.g. Sembla, Gban, Tura, Yaure (Dwyer 1989:54; Williamson 1989:27). The four levels are labelled T (Top), H (High), M (Mid), and L (Low) in this paper, and are written as follows: T = acute accent: á; H = vertical accent: a̍; M = macron: ā; L = grave accent: à. Various glides occur on single vowels, though these are rare, most glides occurring on long vowels." p. 3, §2: "Although the phonology of Jɔ remains to be worked out, enough is known to show that it is similar to other Mande languages. On the surface it has only open syllables." p. 4, §2.1: "[r] and [d] probably do not contrast. new_statements.rule_in_words: Jɔ/Jowulu is described as a tone language with four level tones (T, H, M, L) plus glides; Carlson never states where word stress falls. 'Stressed'/'unstressed vowel' appears only as a conditioning environment for [r]~[d] allophony, for vowel elision yielding kl/kr/bl clusters, and for [r]-drop of the suffix -rá after monosyllabic verb roots. The examples do not yield a consistent position (mārē: second vowel unstressed; páádòì: vowel after medial d stressed), and Carlson states the phonology 'remains to be worked out' (p. 3).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the stress notion itself is undefined.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, from elicited citation forms and a 1991 field word list (Siranikoroba/Koura, Mali); stress is not part of the transcription, only tone is marked.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: Carlson 1993 describes 'Jɔ' (jowulu) of the arrondissement of Loulouni south of Sikasso, Mali (informant from Siranikoroba, plus Koura) = jowu1238; he identifies Prost's 1958 'Don' (Téna, Burkina Faso) as the same language. Note the tone-count discrepancy: Carlson posits four tone levels, whereas Kim 2003 (SIL) marks three and McPherson 2020 (following Djilla et al. 2004) calls Jowulu a three-tone language. 'Samogho' is a cover term also used for the unrelated-within-Mande Duun/Dzùùngoo (Samogohiri) and Seenku; the Köppe/Solomiac 'dzùùngoo de Samogohiri' volumes are NOT Jowulu.
